question: What is Django REST Framework and why does it exist? It is a toolkit on Django for building Web APIs — serializers, viewsets, browsable API — turning models into REST endpoints with less boilerplate.
title: Django REST Framework Fundamentals
direct_answer: Django REST Framework (DRF) is a toolkit layered on Django for building Web APIs, providing serializers (model <-> JSON), viewsets (CRUD endpoints from a model), authentication/permissions, pagination, filtering, and a browsable API. It exists because building a REST API on raw Django views means hand-writing JSON serialization, validation, pagination, auth, and CRUD routing for every model — repetitive and inconsistent. DRF provides reusable, composable components (serializers, viewsets, routers) that turn a model into a full, consistent REST API with far less boilerplate, while staying Django underneath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand DRF as serializers + viewsets + routers turning models into REST endpoints, and can name the serializer's role (model<->JSON + validation) — not just 'Django for APIs'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing DRF without the serializer (the core piece: model<->JSON + validation) or the viewset (CRUD from a model) — missing what DRF actually automates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame DRF as: serializers (model<->JSON + validation), viewsets (CRUD from a model), routers (URLs), permissions, pagination — turning a model into a REST API with minimal boilerplate.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Django REST Framework (DRF) is a toolkit layered on Django for building Web APIs, providing serializers (model <-> JSON), viewsets (CRUD endpoints from a model), authentication/permissions, pagination, filtering, and a browsable API. It exists because building a REST API on raw Django views means hand-writing JSON serialization, validation, pagination, auth, and CRUD routing for every model — repetitive and inconsistent. DRF provides reusable, composable components (serializers, viewsets, routers) that turn a model into a full, consistent REST API with far less boilerplate, while staying Django underneath. The serializer is the core piece: it converts model instances to/from JSON and enforces validation.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) serializers — the heart of DRF; convert a model instance to JSON (serialization) and JSON to a model instance with validation (deserialization); define fields and validation; (2) viewsets — a class that bundles CRUD operations (list, create, retrieve, update, destroy) for a model; ModelViewSet gives full CRUD from a serializer + queryset; (3) routers — wire a viewset to URLs automatically (DefaultRouter); (4) authentication & permissions — pluggable (TokenAuth, JWT, SessionAuth); permission classes (IsAuthenticated, IsAdminUser, custom); (5) pagination & filtering — PageNumberPagination, LimitOffset, filtering via django-filter; (6) the browsable API — a human-usable HTML view of the API for free; (7) it's Django — models, ORM, auth, middleware all apply.

sections.title: A serializer, a viewset, and a router — a full API in ~15 lines
sections.content:
from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets, routers
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from .models import Article

# (1) SERIALIZER: model <-> JSON + validation. The heart of DRF.
class ArticleSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Article
        fields = ['id', 'title', 'published', 'is_published']

# (2) VIEWSET: full CRUD from a serializer + queryset. Permissions plug in.
class ArticleViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Article.objects.all()
    serializer_class = ArticleSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]      # who can do what

# (3) ROUTER: wires the viewset to URLs automatically.
router = routers.DefaultRouter()
router.register('articles', ArticleViewSet)
#   GET    /articles/        -> list
#   POST   /articles/        -> create
#   GET    /articles/{id}/   -> retrieve
#   PUT    /articles/{id}/   -> update
#   DELETE /articles/{id}/   -> destroy
#   Plus a BROWSABLE API at /articles/ (HTML UI) for free.

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is convention versus flexibility: DRF's ModelViewSet + ModelSerializer gives full CRUD from a few lines, but the defaults hide behavior (auto-generated fields, default permissions); the resolution is that everything is overridable (custom fields, validate_* methods, custom permission classes, action decorators). A second tension: serializers can become a second source of truth alongside models — keeping them in sync and avoiding duplication is a practical concern. The third: DRF is sync-first (Django's heritage); for async-heavy or real-time APIs, FastAPI may fit better, so the framework choice is a design decision.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: DRF is a toolkit on Django for Web APIs: serializers, viewsets, routers, permissions, pagination, browsable API — turning a model into a REST API with minimal boilerplate.
The serializer is the core: model<->JSON conversion + validation; it defines fields and enforces rules.
A viewset bundles CRUD (list/create/retrieve/update/destroy) from a serializer + queryset; ModelViewSet gives full CRUD.
A router wires a viewset to URLs automatically; permissions and authentication are pluggable.
Everything is overridable (custom fields, validate_* methods, permission classes, @action) — convention with an escape hatch.
DRF is sync-first (Django's heritage); for async/real-time APIs, FastAPI may fit better — the choice is a design decision.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Django REST Framework is a toolkit layered on Django for building Web APIs, providing serializers, viewsets, authentication, permissions, pagination, filtering, and a browsable API. It exists because building a REST API on raw Django views means hand-writing JSON serialization, validation, pagination, auth, and CRUD routing for every model — repetitive and inconsistent. DRF provides reusable, composable components that turn a model into a full, consistent REST API with far less boilerplate, while staying Django underneath. The serializer is the core piece: it converts a model instance to JSON and JSON back to a model instance with validation, and it defines the fields and the rules. A viewset bundles CRUD operations — list, create, retrieve, update, destroy — from a serializer and a queryset, and ModelViewSet gives you full CRUD in a few lines. A router wires the viewset to URLs automatically. Permissions and authentication are pluggable — TokenAuth, JWT, SessionAuth, and custom permission classes. And the browsable API gives you a human-usable HTML view of the API for free. The honest tension is convention versus flexibility — the defaults hide behavior, but everything is overridable with custom fields, validate methods, permission classes, and action decorators. And DRF is sync-first because of Django's heritage, so for async-heavy or real-time APIs FastAPI may fit better, which makes the framework choice itself a design decision.

question: How do you implement filtering and pagination in Django REST Framework?
title: DRF Filtering and Pagination
direct_answer: Pagination: set DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS to PageNumberPagination or CursorPagination in settings, or override pagination_class on the ViewSet. Filtering: override get_queryset() manually, or use django-filter with DjangoFilterBackend for declarative filter fields. SearchFilter adds ?search= parameter. OrderingFilter adds ?ordering= parameter. Cursor-based pagination is better for large datasets and real-time feeds than page number pagination.
interviewer_intent: Tests practical API design knowledge — pagination and filtering are in every production API.

sections.title: Pagination and filtering
sections.content:
from rest_framework.pagination import PageNumberPagination, CursorPagination
from rest_framework import filters
from django_filters.rest_framework import DjangoFilterBackend

# Pagination
class StandardPagination(PageNumberPagination):
    page_size = 20
    page_size_query_param = 'page_size'
    max_page_size = 100

class TimelineViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    pagination_class = CursorPagination  # stable for real-time feeds
    ordering = ['-created_at']  # cursor requires stable ordering

# Filtering
class ArticleViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    filter_backends = [
        DjangoFilterBackend,
        filters.SearchFilter,
        filters.OrderingFilter
    ]
    filterset_fields = ['status', 'author', 'category']  # exact match
    search_fields = ['title', 'body']  # text search with ?search=
    ordering_fields = ['created_at', 'title', 'view_count']
    ordering = ['-created_at']  # default ordering

# GET /articles/?status=published&search=python&ordering=-created_at&page=2

# Manual filtering in get_queryset
class ArticleViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    def get_queryset(self):
        qs = Article.objects.all()
        status = self.request.query_params.get('status')
        if status:
            qs = qs.filter(status=status)
        return qs

speakable_v2.hook: Every API needs pagination — and cursor pagination is more stable than page numbers for real-time data.

beats.content: PageNumberPagination is simple: ?page=2. CursorPagination uses a stable cursor position — better for feeds where items can be inserted between page loads.
DjangoFilterBackend with filterset_fields = ['status', 'author'] generates exact-match filters. SearchFilter adds full-text search. OrderingFilter adds sortable columns. All from filter_backends.

speakable_v2.cap: Set max_page_size in your pagination class. Without it, someone can request ?page_size=100000 and load your entire database.
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with PostgreSQL full-text search integration, or custom FilterSet for range filters and lookups.
